summary: This note is a wiki-style overview of the Arena Football League (AFL), the highest level of professional indoor American football in the United States, founded in 1987 by Jim Foster. It covers the league's origins from Foster's 1981 idea and 1986 test game, its schedule and playoff format across seasons, its ownership model shift after bankruptcy, attendance trends, notable incidents such as the 1989 Haering punch, the 2009 season cancellation, and 2016 franchise and expansion news.
one_line: Overview of the Arena Football League, the top US professional indoor football league founded by Jim Foster in 1987, covering its history, format, and recent changes.
key_facts: The Arena Football League was founded in 1987 by Jim Foster and is the highest level of professional indoor American football in the United States.
The AFL is the third longest-running professional football league in North America, after the Canadian Football League and the National Football League.
The AFL is played indoors on a 68-yard field, about half the distance of an NFL field.
Foster conceived of indoor football in 1981 while watching an indoor soccer match at Madison Square Garden, sketching the idea on a 9x12 envelope.
The first arena football test game was played on April 27, 1986, after Foster reached an agreement with NBC for a 'test game'.
The league's founding four teams were the Pittsburgh Gladiators, Denver Dynamite, Washington Commandos, and Chicago Bruisers.
Darrel 'Mouse' Davis was appointed executive director of football operations and was the architect of the league's original wide-open offensive playbooks.

On July 23, 1989, Pittsburgh Gladiators head coach Joe Haering punched commissioner Jim Foster in the jaw during a game against the Chicago Bruisers in Sacramento's Arco Arena, and Haering was suspended without pay.
The single-entity model was adopted in 2010 when the league emerged from bankruptcy, with the league owning the rights to teams, players, and coaches.
In 2010, the first year of the reconstituted league after bankruptcy, average attendance decreased to 8,135, with only Tampa Bay exceeding 13,000 per game.
In 2008, the overall attendance average increased to 12,957, with eight teams exceeding 13,000 per game.
The AFL suspended the entire 2009 season, becoming the second sports league to cancel an entire season after the NHL cancelled the 2004-05 season.
The regular season was extended from 14 games to 16 games from 2001 to 2010 and again from 2016, and was 18 games from 2011 to 2015.
The 1993 All-Star Game was held in Des Moines, Iowa, where the National Conference defeated the American Conference 64–40 in front of a crowd of 7,189.
On January 6, 2016, the league took over ownership and operational control of the Portland Thunder, and on February 3, 2016 the franchise was announced to start from scratch without the Thunder name.
